notes: Invented pre-order vendor cards (doc 23 §5.3). The real Butterfly Labs case (severe, ~12-15 month delays, later an FTC enforcement action, Sep 2014-May 2016) sets the DELAY DISTRIBUTION; the real Avalon Batch 1 (on-time, Jan 2013) sets the 'good outcome' baseline. No real vendor names are used in the cards themselves — Butterfly Labs appears only as a sourced news item (see events_prologue.json bfl_news).

delay_distribution_basis.avalon_batch1: Shipped ~on schedule, Jan 2013, 300 units. Batch 2 (500 units) priced $1,499, planned 1 Mar 2013. [Bitcoin Magazine]
delay_distribution_basis.butterfly_labs: Preorders opened mid-2012 promising ~3 months; volume shipping did not begin until Jun 2013 for orders as early as Mar 2012 — roughly a 12-15 month delay. FTC obtained a TRO/asset freeze Sep 2014; by Sep 2013 over 20,000 consumers had not received paid-for machines; final judgment (largely suspended) Feb/May 2016. [CoinDesk; FTC press release]
delay_distribution_basis.design_choice: No sourced percentage of pre-order customers who got nothing at all exists; the game uses an invented but historically-flavoured distribution: 45% on-time-ish (0-1Q late), 35% moderately late (2-3Q late, the 'BFL zone'), 15% very late (4+Q late), 5% never delivered (refund only, no unit).

vendors.name: Summit Silicon (invented)

refund_pct.source: ≈ typical partial-refund outcome in real ASIC-vendor disputes of this era (BFL's eventual settlement was largely suspended for inability to pay, i.e. worse than 50% — game rounds up slightly for playability)

vendors.seed_note: Resolved with the seeded RNG at order time so golden replays hold (doc 23 §11).

vendors.name: Northgate ASICs (invented)
vendors.seed_note: A second, slightly-worse-odds vendor so the player can compare two pre-order offers side by side, as real 2012-13 buyers often weighed several ASIC startups against each other.

vendors.name: A forum group buy (invented specific thread; the practice itself is real)
vendors.delay_roll_note: REVISION 1 addition. Odds are set slightly worse than the two solo vendors (lower on-time share, higher never share, lower refund on failure) — a group buy adds an extra layer of real-world risk on top of the vendor itself: the organizer/operator running the shared unit (real ASIC.COOP-style arrangements had the operator run the hardware and distribute payouts, so an unreliable or dishonest organizer is a second point of failure a solo pre-order doesn't have).
vendors.real_basis: Group buys of early ASIC hardware were a real, common practice, not an invented mechanic. bitcointalk.org runs a dedicated 'Group Buys' board (board=137) for exactly this — miners coordinating bulk/shared orders to split cost and risk. A directly on-period example: 'ASIC.COOP ASIC MINERS COOPERATIVE' (bitcointalk.org topic 88008, posted 16 Jun 2012) sold 5,000 shares at 1 BTC each in a pooled Butterfly Labs BitForce SC Mini Rig (1 TH/s, $29,899) order, with the operator running the hardware, taking weekly operating costs, and distributing the remaining profits to shareholders — the structural real-world basis for this card's 'half a unit, shared with invented forum friends' framing.
vendors.source: bitcointalk.org board 137 ('Group Buys'); bitcointalk.org topic 88008 ('ASIC.COOP ASIC MINERS COOPERATIVE', 16 Jun 2012)
vendors.seed_note: Cheaper entry point for a cash-constrained early path (Design flag 4 in the report's original pass) — half the price for half the hashrate, with slightly worse delivery odds than going it alone.

conference_contact_effect.description: Taking the 'Go to a conference' money sink (doc 23 §7) before ordering shifts the roll: +10 percentage points from severe_4plus_q/never into on_time_0_1q, reflecting a real-world edge from meeting a vendor's team in person before wiring money.
